'''''Drosera capensis''''' ({{IPAc-en|'|d|r|ɒ|s|ə|r|ə|_|k|ə|ˈ|p|ɛ|n|s|ɪ|s}}), the '''Cape sundew''', is a perennial [[rosette (botany)|rosette]]-forming [[carnivorous plant|carnivorous]] herb in the [[flowering plant]] family [[Droseraceae]]. It is native to the [[Cape Provinces|Cape]] region of South Africa,<ref name=powo>{{cite POWO |title=''Drosera capensis'' L. |id=321806-1 |access-date=28 August 2025}}</ref> where it grows in permanently wet, nutrient-poor habitats. Its elongated, roughly oblong leaves are held semi-erect and have a distinct [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]. It is quite a variable plant with several recognised growth forms, some of which develop a short stem. As in all [[sundew]]s, the leaves are covered in stalked glands that secrete sticky [[mucilage]]. These attract, trap, and digest [[arthropod]] prey, obtaining nutrients that supplement intake from the [[substrate (biology)|substrate]] in which the plant grows. ''D. capensis'' has dramatically mobile leaves that curl around captured prey, preventing its escape and facilitating digestion.

First recorded in the late 17th century, ''D. capensis'' was one of the five ''[[Drosera]]'' species included in the first edition of [[Carl Linnaeus]]' ''[[Species plantarum]]''. A relatively large, 'showy' species that flowers readily and is considered very easy to grow, it was cultivated in Europe as a curiosity from the mid-18th century and is now one of the most widely grown sundews. It has also been extensively studied, including as a potential source of [[bioactive compound]]s of [[pharmacological]] interest, and was the first sundew to undergo [[whole-genome sequencing]]. Although often uncommon and localised in its native range, it has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in several countries following deliberate introductions and is listed as an [[invasive species]] in [[New Zealand]].

==Characteristics==
===Habit===
''D. capensis'' is a perennial [[herbaceous plant|herb]] forming a [[rosette (botany)|rosette]] typically {{cvt|10-15|cm|in|0}} in diameter,<ref name="dow-3">{{cite book |last1=Robinson |first1=Alastair |last2=Gibson |first2=Robert |last3=Gonella |first3=Paulo |last4=McPherson |first4=Stewart |last5=Nunn |first5=Richard |last6=Fleischmann |first6=Andreas |title=Drosera of the World Vol. 3 |date=2017 |publisher=Redfern Natural History Productions |location=Poole, Dorset |isbn=978-1-908787-18-7 |page=1340}}</ref> although occasionally up to {{cvt|30|cm|in}}.<ref name="gibson-2020">{{cite journal |last1=Gibson |first1=Robert |title=''Drosera capensis'' - some variation in cultivation and in the wild |journal=Carnivorous Plant Newsletter |date=December 2020 |volume=49 |issue=4 |pages=173–180 |doi=10.55360/cpn494.rg752 |url=https://cpn.carnivorousplants.org/articles/CPNv49n4p173_180.pdf |access-date=3 May 2025}}</ref> Its narrow, oblong leaves are held semi-erect.<ref name="gibson-2020"/> As in all [[sundew]] species, the [[lamina (botany)|laminae]] are covered with stalked glands ("tentacles") that secrete a sticky [[mucilage]]. These attract, trap, and digest insects and other arthropods as prey. New leaves grow from the centre of the rosette and the remains of old leaves gradually form a short stem, typically around {{cvt|4|cm|in}} in length but sometimes as long as {{cvt|15|cm|in}}.<ref name="gibson-2020" /> The roots are sparse, thickened, and attain a length around {{cvt|15-20|cm|in|0}}, rarely branching.<ref name="dow-3"/><ref name="gibson-1993">{{cite journal |last1=Gibson |first1=R. |title=''Drosera capensis'' - know it and grow it |journal=Veld & Flora |date=June 1993 |volume=79 |issue=2 |pages=54–55 |url=https://journals.co.za/doi/epdf/10.10520/AJA00423203_2493 |access-date=28 May 2025}}</ref> In summer, the plant produces one or two relatively tall inflorescences, each with between 15 and 30 flowers. The petals are typically pale purple.

====Growth forms====
''D. capensis'' is quite variable across its range, and several distinct forms have been informally identified.<ref name="gibson-2020" /> In his 1986 book ''[[Insect-eating Plants and How to Grow Them]]'', [[Adrian Slack]] referred to two forms: 
*"typical" form with laminae up to {{cvt|8|mm|in}} wide and {{cvt|38|mm|in}} long, flowers up to {{cvt|2|cm|in}} wide, which develops a stem and a semi-trailing habit
*"narrow-leaf" form, smaller overall, with narrower leaves, minimal stem formation, and smaller flowers that are produced earlier<ref name="slack-1986">{{cite book |last1=Slack |first1=Adrian |title=Insect-eating Plants and How to Grow Them |date=1986 |publisher=Alphabooks |location=Sherborne, Dorset |isbn=0-906670-42-X |page=44 |url=https://archive.org/details/insecteatingplan0000slac/page/44/mode/2up |access-date=5 May 2025}}</ref>

[[Peter D'Amato]] described four forms in his 1998 book ''[[The Savage Garden: Cultivating Carnivorous Plants]]'':
*''D. capensis'' - "typical" with red-tentacled leaves {{cvt|3-6|in|cm}} long, and forming a scrambling stem
*''D. capensis'' - "narrow" with narrow leaves and less tendency to form a stem
*''D. capensis'' - "alba" similar to the "narrow" form but with white flowers and pale tentacles
*''D. capensis'' - "red" similar to the "narrow" form but entirely reddish-maroon in colour when growing in bright light, with deep pink flowers<ref name="d'amato-1998">{{cite book |last1=D'Amato |first1=Peter |title=The Savage Garden: Cultivating Carnivorous Plants |date=1998 |publisher=Tenspeed Press |isbn=0-89815-915-6 |pages=127–129}}</ref>

Gibson also noted occasional plants of the narrow-leaved form with enlarged [[bract]]eoles with insect-trapping hairs, and some red-leaved plants developing a row of insect-trapping hairs on the petals.<ref name="gibson-2020" />

===Leaves and carnivory===
====Morphology====
''D. capensis'' has elongated, roughly rectangular leaves with a distinct [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] typically similar in length to the lamina,<ref name="wang-2015">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Dong-Hui |last2=Wang |first2=Dong-Qi |last3=Cui |first3=Yi-Wei |last4=Yang |first4=Lu |last5=Gu |first5=Xiao-Di |last6=Song |first6=Wen-Fei |last7=Li |first7=Feng |title=Photoperiod regulates Cape Sundew (''Drosera capensis'') gland secretion and leaf development |journal=Carnivorous Plant Newsletter |date=2015 |volume=44 |issue=4 |pages=197–203 |doi=10.55360/cpn444.wd847 |url=https://cpn.carnivorousplants.org/articles/CPNv44n4p197_203.pdf |access-date=3 May 2025}}</ref> although in some growth forms it may be significantly longer.<ref name="gibson-2020" /> [[Vernation]] is geniculate-involute,<ref name="fleischmann-2018" />{{rp|7}} the lamina first unfolding from the petiole, and the lamina margin and tentacles unfurling outward from the leaf axis.

In section, the petiole is a narrow trapezoid with a thickened midrib on the lower (abaxial) side. It has a covering of fine, translucent white hairs, sparse on the upper (adaxial) surface and sparse to moderate on the lower surface.<ref name="dow-3" />

The lamina is usually slightly wider than the petiole.<ref name="gibson-2020" /> It has long, glandular hairs (tentacles) around the margins of the upper surface, surrounding shorter glandular hairs in the middle of the lamina. The lower surface of the lamina lacks tentacles but has a sparse to moderate covering of shorter, translucent white, spreading hairs.<ref name="dow-3" />

[[File:Closeup of Drosera capensis 9.jpg|thumb|alt=Refer to caption|Brown, triangular [[stipule]]s at the leaf base in ''D. capensis'']]
''D. capensis'' has conspicuous [[stipule]]s at the leaf bases; these are brown and roughly triangular,<ref name="dow-3" /> membranous, with the apex intact or slightly divided into [[seta]]e, {{cvt|6-8|mm|in}} long and {{cvt|4-5|mm|in}} wide.<ref name="diels-1906">{{cite book |last1=Diels |first1=Ludwig |title=Droseraceae ''in Engler, A.'' Das Pflanzenreich |date=1906 |publisher=W. Engelmann |location=Leipzig |page=100 |language=de,la |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/20851783#page/106/mode/1up |access-date=3 May 2025}}</ref>{{efn|"{{lang|la|Stipulae membranaceae, ovatae, concavae, apice in setas nonnullas solutae, ceterum integrae vel subintegrae, 6 — 8 mm longae, 4 — 5 mm latae}}"}}

''Drosera'' species exhibit numerous different types of glandular trichomes (hairs). In addition to the large "tentacles" involved in prey capture, leaves of ''D. capensis'' have two types of microscopic glandular trichomes: Type 3 trichomes (short, unbranched, biseriate, stalk two- or three-celled, gland vertically divided) and Type 10 trichomes (unbranched short glandular hairs, stalk biseriate, gland multicellular).<ref name="länger-1995">{{cite journal |last1=Länger |first1=R |last2=Pein |first2=I |last3=Kopp |first3=B |title=Glandular hairs in the genus ''Drosera'' (Droseraceae) |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |date=1995 |volume=194 |issue=3/4 |pages=163–172 |doi=10.1007/BF00982853 |jstor=23643060 |bibcode=1995PSyEv.194..163L }}</ref>

====Movement and prey capture====
[[File:Drosera Capensis eating a fruit fly.webm|thumb|alt=A fly is captured by the leaf of ''D. capensis'': First, the tentacles near the fly bend toward it, then the whole leaf enfolds the fly. |Time-lapse video of ''D. capensis'' leaf movement following prey capture]]
Like all sundews, ''D. capensis'' attracts, captures, and digests prey by means of stalked glandular [[trichome]]s (hairs or tentacles) that secrete droplets of sticky mucilage containing digestive enzymes. When a potential prey item contacts the marginal tentacles, they bend toward the centre of the leaf, bringing the prey item into contact with more tentacles. Adjacent marginal tentacles also move toward the prey, making prey escape more difficult and facilitating digestion.<ref name="williams-1976">{{cite journal |last1=Williams |first1=Stephen E. |title=Comparative Sensory Physiology of the Droseraceae - The Evolution of a Plant Sensory System |journal=Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society |date=June 1976 |volume=120 |issue=3 |pages=187–204 |jstor=986558 }}</ref>

''D. capensis'' is among the sundew species in which the lamina itself also exhibits significant movement. When prey is detected, the leaf blade slowly bends inwards around the location of the prey, enfolding it. In ''D. capensis'', the leaf can bend through more than 180°, "rolling" around the prey. The extent to which the leaf bends depends on the location of the prey; the closer the prey to the tip of the leaf, the more pronounced the bending response.<ref name="bopp-weber-1981">{{cite journal |last1=Bopp |first1=Martin |last2=Weber |first2=Inge |title=Hormonal regulation of the leaf blade movement of ''Drosera capensis'' |journal=Physiologia Plantarum |date=1981 |volume=53 |issue=4 |pages=491–496 |doi=10.1111/j.1399-3054.1981.tb02738.x|bibcode=1981PPlan..53..491B }}</ref>

Experiments involving treatment of leaves of ''D. capensis'' with an [[auxin]] ([[indole-3-acetic acid]]) and an auxin transport inhibitor ([[2,3,5-triiodobenzoic acid]]) demonstrated that bending of the leaf is caused by a hormonal growth stimulus transported from the tip of the leaf to the bending point and induced by a signal originating at the location of the prey.<ref name="bopp-weber-1981" />

====Mucilage====
The mucilage produced by the glandular tentacles of ''D. capensis'' is an aqueous solution of about 4% of an acidic [[polysaccharide]] containing [[xylose]], [[mannose]], [[galactose]], [[glucuronic acid]], and [[organosulfate|ester sulphate]] in the ratio 1:6:6:6:1, with a [[pH]] of 5. It is viscous—about six times more viscous than water at {{cvt|20|C|F}}—and so sticky that when fresh, it can form threads up to {{cvt|1|m|ft}} long.<ref name="rost-schauer-1977">{{cite journal |last1=Rost |first1=Karl |last2=Schauer |first2=Roland |title=Physical and chemical properties of the mucin secreted by ''Drosera capensis'' |journal=Phytochemistry |date=1977 |volume=16 |issue=9 |pages=1365–1368 |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)88783-X|bibcode=1977PChem..16.1365R }}</ref>

===Flowers and seeds===
[[File:Drosera capensis inflorescence Darwiniana.jpg|alt=An inflorescence on a thin stem with two spent flowers, one open pink flower, and a curling row of unopened flower buds|thumb|Inflorescence of ''D. capensis'']]
The plant produces one, two, or occasionally three inflorescences,<ref name="dow-3" /><ref name="diels-1906" /> typically {{cvt|15-25|cm|in}} tall, but sometimes only {{cvt|10|cm|in}} or up to {{cvt|35|cm|in}}. The scape, [[pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s, and abaxial surface of the [[sepal]]s have a moderate covering of coarse, translucent white, spreading hairs.<ref name="dow-3" />

Each inflorescence bears numerous flowers, usually 15–30+<ref name="dow-3" /> but occasionally as few as 6.<ref name="diels-1906" /> The five-petalled flowers are arranged along one side of the [[peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] and open sequentially, starting at the base.<ref name="lecoufle-1990">{{cite book |last1=Lecoufle |first1=Marcel |translator-last=Farrar |translator-first=P.J. |title=Carnivorous Plants: Care and Cultivation |date=1990 |publisher=Cassell Illustrated |isbn=978-0-7137-2185-0 |page=66}}</ref> The pedicels are semi-erect and {{cvt|3-6|mm|in}} long. Sepals are [[obovate]], {{cvt|3-5|mm|in}} long and {{cvt|1.5-2|mm|in}} wide, and usually green.<ref name="dow-3" /> Petals are also obovate, {{cvt|8-15|mm|in}} long and {{cvt|5-12|mm|in}} wide and typically pale purple, sometimes with a darker purple base.<ref name="dow-3" /> Forms with dark purple or white petals also exist.<ref name="gibson-2020" /><ref name="d'amato-1998" />

[[File:Drosera capensis, red plant, exhibition in Botanical garden Brno (2011) (5).JPG|thumb|alt=Refer to caption|Fully open flower of ''D. capensis'']]
The five [[stamen]]s are {{convert|3-4|mm|in}} long with a pink [[filament (botany)|filament]] and yellow [[anther]]s and pollen. The apex of the filament is expanded between the anthers. The ovary is green, [[obovate|obovoid]], {{cvt|2|mm|in}} long, and {{cvt|1.5-2|mm|in}} in diameter.<ref name="dow-3" /> The three purple [[style (botany)|style]]s are {{cvt|4-8|mm|in}} long,<ref name="dow-3" /> forked at the base and lie subhorizontal, expanding into stigmata that are cylindrical to irregularly obovate.<ref name="gibson-2020" />

The flowers are [[self-fertile]] and [[autogamous]] (self-pollinating). Copious seeds are produced in [[dehiscent]] capsules, ripening 4–5 weeks after pollination.<ref name="gibson-2020" /> The seeds are dark brown, shiny, and cylindrical with tapered ends, approximately {{cvt|0.7-1.0|mm|in}} long and {{cvt|0.1-0.2|mm|in}} in diameter. The [[testa (botany)|testa]] is deeply ridged longitudinally, with slightly shallower transverse ridges forming a net-patterned (reticulated) surface.<ref name="dow-3" />

===Genetics===
''D. capensis'' is a [[tetraploid]] species with a [[chromosome number]] of 2''n''=40.<ref name="rivadavia-2005">{{cite journal |last1=Rivadavia |first1=Fernando |title=New chromosome numbers for ''Drosera'' L. (Droseraceae) |journal=Carnivorous Plant Newsletter |date=September 2005 |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=85–91 |doi=10.55360/cpn343.fr964 |url=https://cpn.carnivorousplants.org/articles/CPNv34n3p85_91.pdf |access-date=27 May 2025}}</ref>

The red-leaved form of the species was the first sundew—and the first carnivorous plant from order [[Caryophyllales]], which also includes ''[[Nepenthes]]'', ''[[Aldrovanda]]'', ''[[Drosophyllum]]'' and ''[[Dionaea muscipula|Dionaea]]''—to undergo [[whole-genome sequencing]].<ref name="gibson-2020" /><ref name="butts-2016">{{cite journal |last1=Butts |first1=Carter T. |last2=Bierma |first2=Jan C. |last3=Martin |first3=Rachel W. |title=Novel proteases from the genome of the carnivorous plant Drosera capensis: Structural prediction and comparative analysis |journal=Proteins: Structure, Function, and Bioinformatics |date=October 2016 |volume=84 |issue=10 |pages=1517–1533 |doi=10.1002/prot.25095|pmid=27353064 |pmc=5026580 }}</ref> The genome spans a total of 264 [[base-pair|Mbp]].<ref name="butts-2016" />

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:D capensis kromme river.jpg|thumb|alt=Refer to caption|A stand of ''Drosera capensis'' growing alongside the [[Kromme River]], [[Cederberg]], South Africa]]
The native range of ''D. capensis'' spans the full width of the south coast of the [[Western Cape]] province, extending north from [[Cape Town]] to [[Gifberg]] and eastward into the [[Eastern Cape]] as far as [[Port Elizabeth]].<ref name="gibson-2020" /> It has been reported from [[Brandfontein]] near [[Bredasdorp]]; [[Elim, Western Cape|Elim]]; [[Houwhoek Pass|Houwhoek]]; [[Ceres, South Africa|Ceres]]; near the [[N7 (South Africa)|N7 road]] between [[Clanwilliam, South Africa|Clanwilliam]] and [[Citrusdal]]; the [[Verlorenvlei River]]; [[Hermanus]]; [[Paarl]]; [[Table Mountain National Park]]; [[Diep River, Cape Town|Diep River]] near [[Plumstead, Cape Town|Plumstead]]; [[Riversdale, South Africa|Riversdale]] including the [[Korinte River]]; [[Franschhoek]]; [[Jonkershoek Nature Reserve|Jonkershoek]]; [[Viljoenspas]]; the [[Tradouw Pass]]; [[Nuwekloof Pass (Western Cape)|Tulbagh Kloof]]; [[Theewaterskloof Local Municipality|Theewaterskloof]]; and [[Bainskloof Pass|Bainskloof]].<ref name="obermeyer-1970">{{cite book |last1=Obermeyer |first1=A. A. |author1-link=Anna Amelia Obermeyer |editor1-last=Codd |editor1-first=L.E.W. |editor2-last=de Winter |editor2-first=B. |editor3-last=Killick |editor3-first=D.J.B. |editor4-last=Rycroft |editor4-first=H.B. |title=Droseraceae ''in'' Flora of Southern Africa: the Republic of South Africa, Basutoland, Swaziland and South West Africa, Volume 13 |date=1970 |publisher=Govt. Printer |location=Pretoria |page=199 |isbn=978-0-621-04737-0 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/209567#page/211/mode/1up |access-date=27 May 2025}}</ref><ref name="dow-3" />

It is found at elevations from {{cvt|0-1800|m|ft|-2}} in permanently wet habitats such as [[seep (hydrology)|seep]]s, the edges of creeks and coastal wetlands, and in sheltered locations such as cliff bases. The plant grows in peaty or sandy soils, on moss-covered rocks, in [[quartzite]] rubble or in ''[[Sphagnum]]'' moss beds.<ref name="dow-3" /><ref name="gibson-2020" /> At seepage sites it may grow on near-vertical rock faces.<ref name="dow-3" /><ref name="boaz">{{cite web |last1=Boaz |first1=Ng |title=''Drosera capensis'' in the wild |url=https://www.fierceflora.com/drosera-capensis-2/ |website=Fierce Flora |date=16 October 2023 |access-date=27 May 2025}}</ref> Despite its reputation as a weed in cultivation,<ref name="d'amato-1998" /> ''D. capensis'' is often uncommon or localised in its native habitat, although it may become locally numerous where competing vegetation is suppressed, such as following a fire.<ref name="gibson-2020" />

==Taxonomy==
===Botanical history===
====Pre-Linnaean====
[[File:Drosera capensis burman 1738.jpg|thumb|alt=A detailed and quite accurate line drawing of Drosera capensis with other plant drawings|''Drosera capensis'' illustrated in Burman's ''[[Rariorum Africanarum Plantarum]]'', 1739]]

''D. capensis'' was first introduced to Western botany around the end of the [[17th century]]. [[Paul Hermann (botanist)|Paul Hermann]] became one of the first botanists to collect herbarium specimens of plants from the [[Dutch Cape Colony|Cape of Good Hope]] during his voyage to [[Dutch Ceylon|Ceylon]] in April 1672,<ref name="britten-1920">{{cite journal |last1=Britten |first1=James |title=Some Early Cape Botanists and Collectors |journal=Journal of the Linnean Society of London, Botany |date=1920 |volume=45 |issue=301 |pages=29–51 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.1920.tb00118.x}}</ref><ref name="glen-2010">{{cite book |last1=Glen |first1=H.F. |last2=Germishuizen |first2=G. |title=Botanical exploration of southern Africa. ''Strelitzia'' 26 |date=2010 |publisher=[[South African National Biodiversity Institute]] |location=Pretoria |isbn=978-1-919976-54-9 |edition=2 |url=https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/2010_strelitzia26.pdf}}</ref>{{rp|65}}  but his plan for a detailed publication on African plants was not fulfilled prior to his death in 1695<ref name="rauschert-1970" />{{rp|307}} and his collection later became fragmented.<ref name="glen-2010" />{{rp|210}} A catalogue of plants observed by Hermann at the Cape was published in 1737, as an appendix to [[Johannes Burman]]'s ''[[Thesaurus Zeylanicus]]''.<ref name="burman-1737">{{cite book |last1=Burman |first1=Johannes |title=Thesaurus Zeylanicus, exhibens plantas in insula Zeylana nascentes; Inter quas Plurimae novae species, & genera inveniuntur. Omnia Iconibus illustrata, ac descripta / cura & studio Joannis Burmanni, Med. Doct. & Botanices Professoris in Horto Medico Amstelaedamensi |date=1737 |publisher=Janssonio-Waesbergios & Salomonem Schouten |location=Amsterdam |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/medias/ce/46/34/02/ce463402-3300-476b-8ff1-a3eb5580e431/files/1499.pdf |language=la |access-date=20 May 2025}}</ref>{{efn|Entitled ''Catalogus plantarum Africanum, quas Paulus Hermannus Botanices Professor, ad Caput Bonae Spei olim observavit'' (Catalogue of African plants, which Paul Hermann, Professor of Botany, once observed at the Cape of Good Hope)}} A plant that could be ''D. capensis''{{efn|Cited as such by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his description in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', 1753.}} is listed among the four types of ''Ros Solis'' (sundew) in this work, described as ''Ros Solis Africanus, folio lato, & longo'' (African sundew, broad and long leaf).<ref name="burman-1737" />{{rp|19}} Sources disagree as to whether all the listed plants were actually collected by Hermann, or merely observed.<ref name="rauschert-1970">{{cite journal |last1=Rauschert |first1=Stephan |title=Das Herbarium von Paul Hermann (1646-1695) in der Forschungsbibliothek Gotha |journal=Hercynia N.F. |date=1970 |volume=7 |issue=4 |language=de |pages=301–328 |doi=10.25673/93752 |url=https://opendata.uni-halle.de/bitstream/1981185920/95708/1/hercynia_volume_7_2082.pdf |access-date=19 May 2025}}</ref>

The third volume of [[John Ray]]'s ''[[Historia Plantarum (Ray book)|Historia Plantarum]]'', published in 1704, included descriptions of three African ''Ros Solis'', which were attributed to [[William Sherard]]. Among these is ''Ros Solis Africanus, foliis praelongis, caule nudo altissimo'' (African sundew, very long leaves, very tall bare stem).<ref name="ray-1704">{{cite book |last1=Ray |first1=John |title=Historia plantarum: species hactenus editas aliasque insuper multas noviter inventas & descriptas complectens. Tomus tertius. |date=1704 |location=London |language=la |page=515 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/126270#page/531/mode/1up |access-date=19 May 2025}}</ref>{{efn|Sherard was a friend of Hermann from the early 1680s and received specimens from him, including some from the Cape; he also assisted in the posthumous publication of Hermann's work.<ref name="glen-2010" />{{rp|211}}}}

A detailed engraving and description of ''D. capensis'' was given in Burman's 1739 ''[[Rariorum Africanarum Plantarum]]'' (Decas Octava) under the [[phrase name]] "{{lang|la|Drosera foliis ad radicem longissimis, floribus spicatis}}".<ref name="burman-1739">{{cite book |last1=Burman |first1=Johannes |title=Rariorum Africanarum Plantarum, Ad vivum delineatarum, Iconibus ad descriptionibus illustratarum decas octava |date=1739 |publisher=Henricum Boussiere |location=Amsterdam |language=la |pages=208–209 |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/medias/9b/97/43/8a/9b97438a-fee5-4819-ab8e-3146e655a211/files/4792.pdf |access-date=20 May 2025}}</ref> Burman stated that he obtained the specimen from [[Laurent Garcin]] in whose collection it was described as "{{lang|la|Ros Solis Capensis, foliis longissimis, circinnatis, floribus purpureis, spicatis}}".{{efn|"{{lang|la|a Dom. Garcin haec cum subsequente ex ejus Herbario mecum est communicata, quae ipsi vocatur Ros Solis Capensis foliis longissimis, circinnatis, floribus purpureis, spicatis.}}"}}

====Linnaeus and later 18th century====
''D. capensis'' was one of the five species of ''Drosera'' included in [[Carl Linnaeus]]' 1753 ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', where he gave the short description "{{lang|la|DROSERA scapis radicatis, foliis lanceolatis}}" and the origin "{{lang|la|habitat in [[Aethiopia]]}}". Linnaeus cited as synonymous with ''D. capensis'', the three earlier descriptions noted above.<ref name="linnaeus-1753">{{cite book |last1=Linnaeus |first1=Carl |title=Species plantarum |date=1753 |publisher=Laurentii Salvii |location=Stockholm |language=la |page=282 |edition=1 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/84235#page/296/mode/1up |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref>

[[File:African Drosera (Eden, John Hill, 1757).jpg|thumb|alt=An inaccurate engraving labelled 'African Drosera' showing a plant with pointed, hairy leaves and a symmetrical flower scape|'African Drosera' (''Drosera capensis'') illustration from Plate 25 of ''[[Eden, or a compleat body of gardening]]'', 1757]]

In 1757, [[John Hill (botanist)|John Hill]] gave a lengthy description of the species in English in the illustrated work ''[[Eden, or a compleat body of gardening]]''.<ref name="hill-1757">{{cite book |last1=Hill |first1=John |title=Eden: or, a compleat body of gardening |date=1757 |publisher=T. Osborne |location=Gray's Inn, London |pages=294–295 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/131789#page/354/mode/1up |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref> Hill did not use Linnaeus' [[binomial name]], giving only the title "African Drosera", but the introduction makes clear which species is referred to:

{{Blockquote|We propose here to the Curious a little Plant, singular in its Kind for a Garden Ornament; and though a Native of the warmest Parts of ''Africa'', capable of bearing unhurt our Climate in a full Exposure.

Most who have treated of the ''African'' Plants have named it. {{Smallcaps|Herman}} calls it, {{lang|la|Ros solis folio lato :}} and {{Smallcaps|Ray}}, {{lang|la|Ros solis foliis praelongis}}.—{{Smallcaps|Linnaeus}}, who has adopted for the Genus the Name ''Drosera'', adds as the Distinction of this Species, {{lang|la|foliis lanceolatis, scapis radicatis :}} Lanceolate leav'd Drosera, with the Flower-stalk naked from the Root.

It is not unlike in the general Form to the Sundews of ''Europe''; but larger, and more conspicuous than them all; and of a finer Colour.}}

Hill included cultivation details, noting that "Mr. ''Sherrard'' from Seeds pick out of the Heads of Specimens, of the Plant from the ''Cape'', raised several promising Roots upon a Bog" and that the plant could be grown alongside ''[[Sarracenia]]''.<ref name="hill-1757" />

The engraving{{efn|This is signed 'B. Cole sculp.', possibly [[Benjamin Cole (instrument maker)|Benjamin Cole]]}} in Hill's work of ''D. capensis''—which was later described by [[Peter Jonas Bergius]] as {{lang|la|mala}} ('bad')<ref name="bergius-1767">{{cite book |last1=Bergius |first1=Peter Jonas |title=Descriptiones plantarum ex Capite Bonae Spei, cum differentiis specificis, nominibus trivialibus, et synonymis auctorum justis. Secundum systema sexuale ex autopsia concinnavit Atque solicite digessit |date=1767 |publisher=Laur. Salvii |location=Stockholm |language=la |page=81 |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/records/item/13844-descriptiones-plantarum-ex-capite-bonae-spei |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref>—appears alongside another carnivorous plant, ''[[Nepenthes]]''. There is no indication that Hill was aware of this shared characteristic, and he surmises (incorrectly) that both plants' fluid secretions serve to "discharge redundant Moisture".<ref name="hill-1757" />

''D. capensis'' is the only ''Drosera'' species listed in the short dissertation ''Flora capensis'' defended by Linnaeus' pupil [[Carl Wänman]] in 1759;<ref name="linnaeus-1759">{{cite book |last1=Linnaeus |first1=Carl |title=Flora capensis ''in'' Amoenitates academicae, seu, Dissertationes variae physicae, medicae, botanicae :antehac seorsim editae : nunc collectae et auctae: cum tabulis aeneis |date=1759 |volume=v.5 |publisher=Godofredum Kiesewetter |location=Stockholm |language=la |page=365 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15497#page/368/mode/1up |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref>  it was also the only ''Drosera'' included in Bergius' 1767 ''[[Descriptiones plantarum ex Capite Bonae Spei]]''.<ref name="bergius-1767" />

Another of Linnaeus' students, [[Carl Thunberg]], spent three years at the Cape between April 1772 and March 1775. Thunberg carried out botanical exploration of the area while also learning Dutch as preparation for onward travel to Japan, which under the [[Sakoku|Sakoku isolationist policy]] of the [[Edo period]] was only open to the Dutch.<ref name="glen-2010" />{{rp|57}} ''D. capensis'' appeared in two works published by Thunberg at the end of the 18th century. In ''[[Prodromus plantarum Capensium]]'' it is listed among four species of ''Drosera'' collected by Thunberg at the Cape between 1772 and 1775, with the short description {{lang|la|D. caule erecto bifido, foliis lanceolatis}} (D. erect, bifurcated stem; lanceolate leaves).<ref name="thunberg-1794">{{cite book |last1=Thunberg |first1=Carl |title=Prodromus plantarum Capensium :quas in promontorio Bonæ Spei Africes, annis 1772-1775 collegit, pars prior |date=1794 |publisher=Joh. Edman |location=Uppsala |language=la |page=57 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/1817#page/69/mode/1up |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref> In 1797 Thunberg published ''Dissertatio botanica de Drosera'' (defended by his student Daniel Haij) which gave a structured treatment of the ten species then included within genus ''Drosera''.<ref name="thunberg-1797">{{cite book |last1=Thunberg |first1=Carl |title=Dissertatio botanica de ''Drosera'' |date=1797 |publisher=Joh. Edman |location=Uppsala |language=la |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/records/item/14488-dissertatio-botanica-de-drosera |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref>{{efn|This includes ''D. lusitanica'' which is now placed in the monotypic genus ''[[Drosophyllum]]'' and ''D. roridula'' which is now ''[[Roridula]]''}} Section 5 of this work ({{lang|la|Characteres specierum}}) provided an infrageneric arrangement of ''Drosera'' based on characteristics of the inflorescence, in which ''D. capensis'' was placed within the group ''Scapigerae'' (scape-bearing) along with ''[[Drosera cuneifolia|D. cuneifolia]]'', ''[[Drosera rotundifolia|D. rotundifolia]]'' and ''D. longifolia''. The distribution was given as "rarer in the mountains".<ref name="thunberg-1797" />{{efn|"{{lang|la|In Capitae Bonae Spei Africes ... in montibus rarior}}"}}

====19th century====
Thunberg's 1823 ''Flora capensis'' included ''Drosera capensis'' among five species of South African ''Drosera'', giving details of the flowering period (September to November).<ref name="thunberg-1823">{{cite book |last1=Thunberg |first1=Carl |title=Flora Capensis :sistens plantas promontorii Bonae Spei Africes, secundum systema sexuale emendatum, redactas ad classes, ordines, genera et species, cum differentiis specificis, synonymis et descriptionibus |date=1823 |publisher=J. G. Cottae |location=Stuttgart |language=la |pages=278–279 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/21802#page/340/mode/1up |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref>

In 1824, [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] provided the first systematic revision of genus ''Drosera'' in his ''[[Prodromus systematis naturalis regni vegetabilis]]'',<ref name="dow-1">{{cite book |last1=Lowrie |first1=Allen |last2=Nunn |first2=Richard |last3=Robinson |first3=Alastair |last4=Bourke |first4=Greg |last5=McPherson |first5=Stewart |last6=Fleischmann |first6=Andreas |title=''Drosera'' of the World Vol. 1 |date=2017 |publisher=Redfern Natural History Productions |location=Poole, Dorset, England |isbn=978-1-908787-16-3}}</ref> with an infrageneric classification of 32 species into two [[section (botany)|section]]s, each having two [[series (botany)|series]]. De Candolle placed ''D. capensis'' in sect. ''Rorella'' ser. ''Acaules, foliis radicalibus saepius rosulatis'' (Stemless, with radical leaves often rosulate).<ref name="de-candolle-1824">{{cite book |last1=de Candolle |first1=A. P. |title=Prodromus systematis naturalis regni vegetabilis, sive, Enumeratio contracta ordinum generum specierumque plantarum huc usque cognitarium, juxta methodi naturalis, normas digesta |date=1824 |volume=1 |pages=317–319 |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.286 |language=la |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/154273#page/324/mode/1up |access-date=29 November 2024}}</ref>

In 1848, [[Jules Emile Planchon]] published a new treatment of ''Drosera'' in the ''[[Annales des sciences naturelles. Botanique]]''. This covered 88 species arranged into 13 sections based on morphological characteristics, including style division. ''D. capensis'' was placed in section ''Rossolis'', which was characterised by a [[hypogyny|hypogynous]] flower with five [[stamen]]s; three [[style (botany)|style]]s, bifurcated from the base, with a club-shaped, undivided or bi-lobed apex of the stigma; and three pluriovate [[placenta (botany)|placenta]]s.<ref name="Planchon-1848">{{cite journal |last1=Planchon |first1=J. E. |title=Sur les Droséracées |journal=Annales des Sciences Naturelles, Botanique |date=1848 |volume=3 |issue=9 |page=196 |language=fr |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/41549140#page/95/mode/1up |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref>

[[Otto Wilhelm Sonder]] provided a botanical description of the species in English in the 1859 ''Flora capensis'' produced with [[William Henry Harvey]]. This included more specific location details—"Wet places, in subalpine situations, near Capetown: [[Du Toitskloof|Dutoit's-kloof]]; [[Paarlberg]], and [[Tulbagh]] &c."<ref name="sonder-1859">{{cite book |last1=Sonder |first1=Otto Wilhelm |last2=Harvey |first2=William Henry |title=Flora capensis :being a systematic description of the plants of the Cape colony, Caffraria, & Port Natal (and neighbouring territories) |date=1859 |publisher=L. Reeve |location=Kent |pages=76–77 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15231#page/132/mode/1up |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref>

[[File:Drosera capensis spathulata Belg Hort 1880 edit.jpg|alt=Refer to caption|thumb|''Drosera capensis'' and ''[[Drosera spatulata]]'' illustrated in [[La Belgique Horticole]], 1880]]

Messrs. [[Veitch Nurseries|Veitch]] presented the plant to the [[Royal Botanic Society]] in London on 22 April 1874,<ref name="belg-hort-1875">{{cite journal |last1=Morren |first1=Edouarde |title=Droseracées |journal=Belgique Horticole |date=1875 |volume=25 |page=103 |language=fr |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/137823#page/117/mode/1up |access-date=24 May 2025}}</ref> and also introduced it to the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]].<ref name="hooker-1881" />  It was noted among interesting plants reported in 1875 in ''[[La Belgique Horticole]]'':

{{Blockquote|A cold greenhouse plant, of a curious and interesting structure, with long-petioled, linear-oblong, obtuse leaves, and covered with glandular hairs.<ref name="belg-hort-1876">{{cite journal |last1=de Vos |first1=André |title=Enumération méthodique des plantes nouvelles ou intéressantes qui ont été signalées en 1875 |journal=La Belgique Horticole |date=1876 |volume=26 |page=155 |language=fr |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/137779#page/175/mode/1up |access-date=24 May 2025}}</ref>{{efn|"{{lang|fr|Plante de serre froide, d'une curieuse et intéressante structure, à feuilles longuement pétiolées, linéaires-oblongues, obtuses, et couvertes de poils glanduleux.}}"}}}}

In 1880, the same journal published an illustrated note on ''D. capensis'' and ''[[Drosera spatulata|D. spatulata]]'' by [[Charles Jacques Édouard Morren|Édouard Morren]], recommending these ''Drosera'' species as "among the most interesting and easiest to cultivate".{{efn|"{{lang|fr|''on peut recommander le ''Drosera capensis'' et le ''Drosera spathulata'', parmi les plus intéressants et les plus faciles''|italic=unset}}"}} The note provided detailed cultivation information, including observations that the plants require pure water and are [[calcifuge]]s.{{efn|"{{lang|fr|Ils veulent de l'eau fraiche et pure, un sol tourbeux et fangeux, ils ne souffrent pas le calcaire, c'est-à-dire qu'ils sont calcifuges, selon l'expression de [[Charles Louis Contejean|M. Contejean]]}}"}} The illustrations were based on plants grown in greenhouses where they had "thrived for several years, multiplying, and flowering regularly".{{efn|"{{lang|fr|Ces deux plantes sont représentées ici, avec leurs fleurs, d'après des spécimens cultivés dans nos serres particulières où elles prospèrent depuis plusieurs années, multiplient et fleurissent régulièrement.}}"}} Morren described cultivation of the plants in the coolest part of a hothouse, where they were watered via drops of condensation from the roof.<ref name="belg-hort-1880">{{cite journal |last1=Morren |first1=Edouarde |title=Note sur les ''Drosera capensis'' Linn. et ''Drosera spathulata'' Labill. |journal=La Belgique Horticole |date=1880 |volume=30 |page=311 |language=fr |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/137825#page/345/mode/1up |access-date=24 May 2025}}</ref>{{efn|"{{lang|fr|Nous cultivons avec succès les Drosera capensis et spathulala dans la serre chaude, mais à l'extrémité inférieure de la toiture, près des vitres, dans une situation où la température n'est que tempérée. Chaque pot est placé sur une petite étagère, immédiatement sous le bout d'une verne, de manière à recevoir constamment et goutte à goutte l'eau qui s'écoule de la toiture : l'eau se renouvelle sans cesse : elle est très pure, puisqu'elle vient en quelque sorte d'être distillée et ne renferme pas traces de chaux : en outre, elle est fraîche et aérée.}}"}}

[[File:Drosera capensis, Curtis' Botanical Magazine plate 6583.jpg|alt=Refer to caption|thumb|Colour illustration of ''Drosera capensis'' from ''[[Curtis's Botanical Magazine]]'', 1881]]

The plant was illustrated by [[Matilda Smith]] in [[Curtis's Botanical Magazine]] in 1881, along with a description by [[Joseph Dalton Hooker]] noting that it had flowered in July in a cool greenhouse at Kew.<ref name="hooker-1881">{{cite journal |last1=Hooker |first1=Joseph Dalton |title=Tab. 6583 - ''Drosera capensis'' |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |date=October 1881 |volume=107 (s. 3, v. 37) |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/14235#page/152/mode/1up |access-date=24 May 2025}}</ref>

In [[Carl Georg Oscar Drude]]'s 1888 treatment of Droseraceae, ''D. capensis'' was given as one of the example species within subg. ''Ros-solis'' section ''Vagae''.<ref name="drude-1888">{{cite book |author=Drude,  O |editor=Engler, Adolf |editor2=Krause, Kurt |editor3=Pilger, R. |editor4=Prantl, Karl |date= 1888 | title=''Droseraceae''. In: Die Natürlichen Pflanzenfamilien nebst ihren Gattungen und wichtigeren Arten, insbesondere den Nutzpflanzen, unter Mitwirkung zahlreicher hervorragender Fachgelehrten begründet | publisher=W. Engelmann |language=de | url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/4635 |pages=270–272 | doi=10.5962/bhl.title.4635}}</ref>

====20th century====
In 1906, the first true [[monograph#Biology|monograph]] of Droseraceae was published in ''[[Das Pflanzenreich]]'' by German botanist and collector [[Ludwig Diels]].<ref name="dow-1"/> Diels built on Planchon's earlier infrageneric classification and placed ''D. capensis'' within subg. ''Rorella'', section ''Rossolis'', series ''Eurossolis''.<ref name="diels-1906" /> Diels' monograph was still considered the standard reference for Drosera anatomy and morphology more than a century later.<ref name="dow-1" /> It included detailed commentary and illustrations on [[germination]] in ''D. capensis''.<ref name="diels-1906" />{{rp|4}}

===Infrageneric classification===
Since 2019, ''D. capensis'' has been placed within [[Drosera sect. Ptycnostigma|''Drosera'' sect. ''Ptycnostigma'']], under the expanded definition established by [[Andreas Fleischmann|Fleischmann]] et al. based on phylogenetic data. This section contains all African sundews except ''D. regia'' and ''D. indica''.<ref name="fleischmann-2018">{{cite journal |last1=Fleischmann |first1=Andreas |last2=Gonella |first2=Paulo |last3=Rivadavia |first3=Fernando |title=A new sectional name for the Brazilian tetraploid clade of ''Drosera'' subgenus ''Drosera'' |journal=Carnivorous Plant Newsletter |date=2018 |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=4–9 |doi=10.55360/cpn471.af718 |url=https://cpn.carnivorousplants.org/articles/CPNv47n1p4_9.pdf |access-date=27 May 2025}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''D. capensis'' is one of the most widely cultivated sundews.<ref name="gibson-2020" /> It is a relatively large, 'showy' species whose leaves exhibit dramatic movement in response to prey capture.<ref name="gibson-2020" /><ref name="slack-1979">{{cite book |last1=Slack |first1=Adrian |title=Carnivorous Plants |date=1979 |publisher=Alphabooks |location=Poole, Dorset |isbn=0-906670-30-6 |page=136}}</ref><ref name="d'amato-1998" /> It is easily propagated, grows rapidly, readily produces attractive flowers, and is considered very easy to grow.<ref name="gibson-1993" /><ref name="d'amato-1998" /><ref name="cheers-1993">{{cite book |last1=Cheers |first1=Gordon |author1-link=Gordon Cheers |title=Letts Guide to Carnivorous Plants of the World |date=1990 |publisher=Angus & Robertson |isbn=1-85238-124-8}}</ref>

===Growing conditions===
The plant requires warm-temperate conditions and is often grown as a houseplant (on a windowsill or in a terrarium), in a greenhouse, or outside in areas with suitable climate.<ref name="d'amato-1998" /> It can withstand infrequent, short-term exposure to temperatures below freezing; the plant may die back above ground, and re-grow from the roots when warmth returns.<ref name="d'amato-1998" /><ref name="gibson-2020" /><ref name="gibson-1993" /> It prefers full sun but will tolerate partial shade,<ref name="lecoufle-1990" /> and requires permanently moist or wet conditions so is typically grown in a saucer or tray of rainwater.<ref name="lecoufle-1990" /><ref name="gibson-1993" /> Growing media is often peat-based—for example a mixture of peat and sand or [[perlite]]—or live ''[[Sphagnum]]'' moss.<ref name="gibson-1993" /><ref name="d'amato-1998" /><ref name="lecoufle-1990" />

===Propagation===
====Sexual====
''D. capensis'' is readily propagated by seed. The plant is self-fertile and produces hundreds of tiny seeds, which germinate readily on a moist substrate.<ref name="d'amato-1998" /><ref name="gibson-1993" /> In favourable growing conditions seedlings can grow to flowering maturity in a single year.<ref name="gibson-1993" />

====Asexual====
The species can be propagated [[vegetative propagation|vegetatively]] via leaf or root cuttings.<ref name="d'amato-1998" /> Whole leaves can be placed on a moist substrate and will develop plantlets as the original leaf dies;<ref name="gibson-1993" /> alternatively the entire above-surface part of the plant can be removed and replanted, and will often develop new roots, while the original roots form a new growing point.<ref name="gibson-1993" /> Short (1.5–3 cm) sections of root from a healthy plant can be taken as cuttings and replanted, forming new buds in 2–6 weeks.<ref name="lecoufle-1990" /><ref name="cheers-1993" /><ref name="gibson-1993" />

===Pests===
The species has few pests in cultivation,<ref name="lecoufle-1990" /> but can be affected by [[caterpillar]]s<ref name="gibson-1993" /> and by [[aphid]]s,<ref name="gibson-1993" /> which attack the flower stalks.<ref name="lecoufle-1990" /><ref name="jobson-2012" />

==Conservation status==
{{As of|2025|June}}, ''Drosera capensis'' does not have an assessment on the [[IUCN Red List]].<ref name="iucn-2025">{{cite web |title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Version 2025-1 |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org |website=IUCN Red List |publisher=IUCN |access-date=28 June 2025}}</ref> On the [[South African National Biodiversity Institute]]'s [[Red List of South African Plants]] it is listed as 'Least Concern', a categorisation applied automatically because it was not highlighted in screening processes used to select taxa of potential conservation concern for detailed assessment.<ref name="foden-2005">{{cite web |last1=Foden |first1=W. |last2=Potter |first2=L. |title=''Drosera capensis'' L. |url=https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=1776-8 |website=National Assessment: Red List of South African Plants, 2005 |publisher=South African National Biodiversity Institute |access-date=27 May 2025}}</ref> In 2020, as part of a large-scale conservation status assessment of carnivorous plants, it was assessed using IUCN criteria as 'Least Concern'.<ref name="cross-2020" />

==Invasive species==
''Drosera capensis'' has been deliberately introduced to wetland habitat in numerous countries outside its native range, including New Zealand, the United States, Japan, Australia, Brazil and the Azores.<ref name="fleischmann-2023">{{cite journal |last1=Fleischmann |first1=Andreas |title=Carnivorous plants and conservation - the role of carnivorous plant enthusiasts |journal=Carnivorous Plant Newsletter |date=June 2023 |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=99–101 |doi=10.55360/cpn522.af323}}</ref> Many of these locations are ecologically sensitive, and introduced species such as ''D. capensis'' may compete with threatened local flora.<ref name="cross-2020" />{{rp|16}}<ref name="fleischmann-2023"/>

In New Zealand, ''D. capensis'' is listed on the [[National Pest Plant Accord]] register meaning that it is prohibited from sale or commercial propagation under the [[Biosecurity Act 1993]].<ref name="bnz-capensis">{{cite web |title=''Drosera capensis'' |url=https://pierpestregister.mpi.govt.nz/pests-of-concern/pest-details?id=90609 |website=Official New Zealand Pest Register |publisher=Biosecurity New Zealand |access-date=26 May 2025}}</ref> It has become established in the [[Waitākere Ranges]], either due to deliberate planting or via soil contamination from other introduced plants. Its seeds are believed to be distributed by waterfowl.<ref name="heenan-2004">{{cite journal |last1=Heenan |first1=P. B. |last2=de Lange |first2=P. J. |last3=Cameron |first3=E. K. |last4=Ogle |first4=C. C. |last5=Champion |first5=P. D. |title=Checklist of dicotyledons, gymnosperms, and pteridophytes naturalised or casual in New Zealand: Additional records 2001–2003 |journal=New Zealand Journal of Botany |date=2004 |volume=42 |issue=5 |page=799 |doi=10.1080/0028825X.2004.9512931|bibcode=2004NZJB...42..797H }}</ref> The species is subject to 'sustained control' under the [[Conservation Auckland]] Regional Pest Management Plan.<ref name="conservation-auckland">{{cite web |title=''Drosera capensis'' - Cape Sundew |url=https://www.tiakitamakimakaurau.nz/protect-and-restore-our-environment/pests-in-auckland/pest-search/drocap/ |website=Pests in Auckland |publisher=Tiaki Tāmaki Makaurau / Conservation Auckland |access-date=26 May 2025}}</ref>

In [[Mendocino County]] California, [[Albion Bog]]—a raised bog in rare [[dwarf forest]] habitat—has become infested with non-native carnivorous plants as a result of deliberate plantings by enthusiasts from the 1960s onwards.<ref name="d'amato-1988">{{cite journal |last1=D'Amato |first1=Peter |title=A field trip to Mendocino |journal=Carnivorous Plant Newsletter |date=March 1988 |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=15–19, 21 |doi=10.55360/cpn171.pd779 |url=https://cpn.carnivorousplants.org/articles/CPNv17n1p15_19_21.pdf |access-date=26 May 2025}}</ref> ''Drosera capensis'' has formed dense stands, outcompeting the native sundew ''[[Drosera rotundifolia|D. rotundifolia]]'', and conservationists have found it impossible to eradicate.<ref name="fleischmann-2023" />{{rp|99}}<ref name="cross-2020">{{cite journal |last1=Cross |first1=Adam T. |last2=Krueger |first2=Thilo A. |last3=Gonella |first3=Paulo M. |last4=Robinson |first4=Alastair S. |last5=Fleischmann |first5=Andreas S. |title=Conservation of carnivorous plants in the age of extinction |journal=Global Ecology and Conservation |date=2020 |volume=24 |article-number=e01272 |doi=10.1016/j.gecco.2020.e01272|bibcode=2020GEcoC..2401272C |hdl=20.500.11937/84611 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

In Australia, ''D. capensis'' was reported as naturalised at a single site in the [[Royal National Park]], where at least 100 adult plants were observed.<ref name="jobson-2012">{{cite journal |last1=Jobson |first1=Richard W. |last2=Conn |first2=Barry J. |title=''Drosera capensis'' (Droseraceae), a new naturalised record for Australia |journal=Telopea: Journal of Plant Systematics |date=December 2012 |volume=14 |pages=89–92 |doi=10.7751/telopea2012015|bibcode=2012Telop..14...89J }}</ref>

In [[Hawaii|Hawaiʻi]], although not known to be naturalised, it is assessed as a 'high risk' species by the [[Plant Pono]] initiative due to characteristics including its self-fertility; prolific seed production; capacity for hybridisation; rapid growth to maturity; tolerance of a wide range of growing conditions; and ability to regenerate after frost and fire damage.<ref name="plant-pono">{{cite web |title=Drosera capensis |url=https://plantpono.org/hpwra/drosera-capensis/ |website=Plant Pono |publisher=Coordinating Group on Alien Pest Species |access-date=26 May 2025}}</ref>

The species is listed (with a 'low' risk rating) in ''A Global Compendium of Weeds''.<ref name="randall-2017">{{cite book |last1=Randall |first1=Roderick P. |title=A Global Compendium of Weeds |date=2017 |publisher=R. P. Randall (self-published) |location=Perth |isbn=978-0-646-96749-3 |edition=3 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/313645439 |access-date=26 May 2025}}</ref>
